  [quoting @norvid-studies.bsky.social: I should get some bookshelves and spend $5000 on books I have in pdf for no reason]
  [image, alt text: can you create an image of a cozy wooden bookshelf that is populated with all of the books in the attached. pull spines or cover images if possible?]
  [image, alt text: I’ll use the image-generation workflow, first checking the book list and how many distinct titles it contains. If the list is manageable, I’ll try to preserve recognisable cover/spine designs; if it is large, I’ll prioritise an attractive, convincing shelf while keeping the titles as faithful as the medium allows.

The file contains 527 entries, so there is a real tension between “every book is present” and “individual spines remain readable” in one normal-resolution image. I’m treating it as a full, floor-to-ceiling personal library: hundreds of volumes, with the nearer and better-known books given recognisable spine treatments and the remainder represented as distinct volumes rather than trying to force 527 tiny, garbled labels.

The image is rendering now. I’ve weighted the shelf toward the actual shape of the collection—especially the large Pratchett run, then King, Hamilton, Robinson, Vonnegut, Kingsolver, Rowling and Jemisin—and asked it to reserve readable lettering for genuine titles rather than inventing convincing-looking nonsense.]
  [image, alt text: Created a cozy, floor-to-ceiling wooden library inspired by the full 527-entry list. Recognisable titles and author groupings appear on prominent spines; the smaller volumes are deliberately less legible to avoid invented titles. Exact commercial cover artwork wasn’t reproduced, but several spine designs echo the real editions.]

@dave.9000ish.uk: @buildthis.bisks.net can you attempt this browser version?

an in-browser library that takes Title, Authors, ISBN/UID, Last Date Read, Stars and populates a virtual bookshelf, you can click on a book to pull it out to look at cover sourced from open library covers api along with metadata (rating)
  [image, alt text: I think this is a much better medium for the idea than a generated image. The room can be visually atmospheric while the books remain entirely deterministic: every mesh originates from one CSV row, and every visible title is rendered directly from that row. There is then no opportunity for The Thursday Murder Club to wander in uninvited.

I’d build it with Three.js and TypeScript, probably without React for the first version. Three.js already provides the pieces we need: WebGL rendering, canvas-generated textures for exact spine lettering, raycasting for selecting books, and instanced meshes if the collection becomes large. Three.js CanvasTexture, Raycaster, and InstancedMesh cover those main jobs.

The flow would be:

Drop a CSV into the page.
Preview the interpreted fields and filters—read years, format, rating, author and so on.
Choose whether rereads create another copy or merge into one volume with multiple year markers.
Generate enough shelves or bookcases for the selected books.
Walk around, orbit the room, search, filter, or click a book to pull it forward and display its metadata.

For your particular CSV, a proper parser matters because reviews contain commas, quotes and embedded line breaks. Papa Parse can read a local browser File directly, meaning the CSV and reviews need not leave the machine. Papa Parse documentation

For the books themselves, I’d use a layered approach:

Actual front cover when an ISBN resolves through the Open Library Covers API.
A generated spine derived from that cover’s dominant colours, with the exact CSV title and author drawn over it.]
  [image, alt text: A tasteful procedural edition when no cover exists—especially for web fiction and books lacking ISBNs.
Never infer or generate a replacement title.
Cache retrieved covers locally so the room loads quickly after the first visit.

Actual spine photography is rarely available systematically, so synthesising the spine from a genuine front cover is likely the strongest compromise. Front-facing and horizontal books can use the real cover or its visual language; upright books receive an edition-adjacent spine whose typography remains readable.

The room could support several arrangements without regenerating the underlying collection:

Arrangement	Behaviour
Reading chronology	Shelves run from earliest to latest
Year rooms	One wall or bookcase per year
Author	Authors and series remain together
Genre	Colour-coded thematic sections
Rating	Five-star books become front-facing
Physical format	Hardcover, paperback, digital and audio represented differently
Organic	Stable seeded variation: leaning, stacking and front-facing

I’d make the default experience more like exploring a cozy study than playing a first-person game: mouse drag to orbit, scroll to approach, and click to inspect. An optional walking mode could come later. Search could be especially satisfying—the room darkens slightly while matching books glow and the camera moves toward the relevant shelf.

The main design tension is legibility versus realism. From across the room, titles naturally cannot be readable. Rather than enlarging them unrealistically, hovering or approaching a shelf could sharpen the spine textures, while clicking presents the title, author, rating, reading dates and review in a clean side]
